items.title: Items 1 and 2 fetched by ids each carry their own brand
covers: Expected: every item in step 1 carries its brand (catalogBrand with id and brand)
Actual: catalogBrand null no longer returned
items.reason: This is the bug's reproduction step 1 turned into an assertion: before the fix each item came back with `"catalogBrand": null`. Using items 1 and 2, which belong to two different brands (Daybird and Gravitator), proves each item gets its own brand rather than one shared value. Functional is the cheapest layer that runs the real endpoint and EF query against Postgres.

items.title: Each item fetched by ids is identical to the same item fetched on its own
covers: Expected: everything else in the answer is unchanged, the same fields
items.reason: The story's expected result is that the batch answer carries the brand "as in step 2" and that "everything else in the answer is unchanged: the same fields". Comparing each batch item field by field with the single-item endpoint (which already includes the brand) catches both a still-missing brand and any accidental change to other fields (for example a dropped or newly added property from changing the query). Functional runs both real endpoints against the same seeded database.

items.title: An item fetched by ids carries the same brand as in the catalog list
covers: Steps to Reproduce step 2 comparison with the catalog list
items.reason: The bug report names the catalog list as the second reference that already shows the brand. This case ties the batch endpoint to the list endpoint, so the two read paths cannot disagree on an item's brand again. The list is ordered by name, so the item is taken from the list answer rather than assumed to be item 1. Functional is enough: both are plain API reads.
